mechanisms.title: Package README contract and package-group maps
mechanisms.problem: A multi-package harness drifts when each package documents itself differently: ownership of a capability becomes ambiguous, group pages duplicate or contradict package contracts, and a consumer mounts the wrong package or expects an API that the owning package never promised.
triggers: Adding a package, package group, bundle, or library to the repository
Moving a capability between a package group and a runnable bundle
Reviewing a package README or group map for composition correctness
obligations: Every package README carries frontmatter with a one-sentence description and a kind (package-group, package-reference, package-library, package-bundle).
Every English README pairs with a Chinese README and a consistency sidecar; the language switcher is the first body line.

A package-group page states the group's Summary, a Table of Contents, a Packages table with each package's Role and ctx key (or the registration/mount relation), Related documentation, and a Dev Note.
The group page maps the group and defers per-package contract and configuration to that package's README; the group must not restate package internals as a second contract.
A group page must distinguish the swappable contract pieces from runnable compositions: for example core owns the spine but runnable compositions live under packages/bundle.
Package READMEs that expose a ctx key state it; packages that register onto another service state the target instead of inventing a new key.
steps: Choose the document kind and write the frontmatter description before the body.
Write Summary in capability terms, not a file inventory.
Add the Packages table and mark every ctx key or registration relation.
Link only to the authoritative subsystem page and Agent Note for related contracts.
Keep group-level Dev Note for maintainer working context, not for new obligations.
Add the Chinese counterpart and regenerate the pairing record with the repository's translation tooling.

enforcement.implementation: Documentation-review and translation-pairing gates check structure and pairing; there is no checker that proves the group map matches the code's actual ctx keys.
enforcement.trust: The map is trusted only as an index. The owning package README and the generated catalogs are the authority for config and schema.
enforcement.failure: A wrong or stale map sends consumers to the wrong package; no runtime check catches it.
enforcement.exceptions: Archived or experimental packages may use the same shape with a smaller body, but they still declare kind and model experience.

mechanisms.applicability: Any repository with package groups, bundle layers, or capability families. Smaller repositories can collapse the group page but should keep the per-package contract and ctx-key declaration.

migration.strategy: Introduce a template directory with the frontmatter fields and a group-map skeleton; migrate one group at a time and make the per-package README the only place where config and schema are described.
migration.implementation: Create docs/package-template.md plus a lint that checks frontmatter keys and presence of Summary/Table of Contents/Packages/Related documentation/Dev Note; add a pairing check for translated counterparts.
migration.requiredSupport: A documented kind vocabulary, a ctx-key registry or generated catalog, and translation tooling that records per-heading hashes.

positive.scenario: A new group README passes the structural lint and every row's ctx key resolves in the generated catalog.
The English/Chinese pair record is regenerated after a heading change and the pairing check is green.

rejection.scenario: A group README missing frontmatter kind or the Packages table fails the structural check.
A group page restating a package's config table as authoritative is rejected in review and replaced by a link.

recovery.scenario: A stale ctx key is corrected in the package README, the group table is updated, and the generated catalog is re-run.

limitations: The map is prose; no test proves it matches runtime registration.
Translation pairing checks structural hashes, not semantic equivalence.
Kind labels are descriptive; nothing prevents a library from carrying a bundle-shaped README.

mechanisms.title: Capability seams: one provider per service, exclusive names and inert seams
mechanisms.problem: If two packages can silently serve the same capability, routing becomes load-order dependent and a deployment cannot tell which backend executed a request. If a seam ships without a provider, consumers may silently do nothing instead of declaring the capability unavailable.
triggers: Introducing a new ctx.* service or replacing its backend
Mounting a second implementation of an existing service
Registering a route, extension, or provider name that another package may also claim
obligations: A seam package defines the service contract, capability vocabulary, and typed errors; it does not register a provider or a model-facing tool itself.
Exactly one provider registers each service per context; loading a second implementation throws the standard duplicate-service error.
A seam without a provider is inert: the key is absent or the capability kind simply has no UI affordance; it must not pretend to work.
Provider replacement must not change the consumer request or the model-visible response; provider-owned coordinates (workspace URI, terminal platform) travel in the result.

Exclusive ownership is declared where it exists: LSP reserves each file extension to one provider, telemetry accepts one backend, subagent providers register under unique names, and browser-use owns exclusive named provider registration.
A route another adapter already owns fails plugin loading rather than silently replacing it.
Duplicate endpoints, namespaces, schema keys, or invocation ids are rejected before anything becomes callable.
steps: Name the service and enumerate the capability union and closed error codes.
Require providers to register through the service with an explicit id and to return a stable capability object.
Make the consumer switch on the capability kind and hide the affordance when no provider implements it.
Reject duplicates atomically at registration, before mutating any registry state.
Test that a second provider fails and that the seam alone produces the documented unavailable behavior.

enforcement.mode: automatic for duplicate registration; implementation + review for provider transparency and seam inertness
enforcement.implementation: Cordis duplicate-service errors and per-registry duplicate checks (LSP extension reservation, telemetry single backend, typert duplicate package-face/schema/endpoint, LLM route collision) reject registration automatically. Provider replacement preserving the consumer request/model-visible response and seam-alone inertness are implemented per capability and verified by their packages/tests or review; they are not one registry-wide guarantee.
enforcement.trust: Automatic only for same-process duplicate/name collision rejection at registration. Request/response invariance across providers and the absence of a silent fallback when no provider exists depend on each seam's implementation, consumer code and review; the registry cannot prove them.
enforcement.failure: Duplicate load throws and the composition must be fixed; an unregistered seam leaves consumers with no capability, which should be surfaced as unavailable rather than retried silently. A provider that changes consumer-visible shape or a seam that invents a fallback is an implementation/review defect, not caught by duplicate registration.
enforcement.exceptions: A deployment-configured selector above registrations is named as intended future work for relaxing exclusive extension ownership; it is not implemented.

mechanisms.applicability: Any service with interchangeable backends (filesystem, shell, sandbox, directory picker, LSP, web fetch, spill storage, telemetry, subagent providers).

migration.strategy: Extract the interface first, keep the shipped implementation as one provider, then add alternative providers behind the same contract. Preserve the consumer-visible request/result shape across providers.
migration.implementation: Declare an abstract service plus a merge-extensible capability map; register providers as effects; add a registration test that loads two providers and asserts the duplicate error.
migration.requiredSupport: A DI container with duplicate-service semantics, a generated ctx-key catalog, and a composition test harness.

positive.scenario: Mounting one directory-picker backend resolves ctx.directoryPicker and capability() returns the declared kind.
Mounting the LSP seam with a stdio provider routes .ts queries without changing the consumer call.

rejection.scenario: Mounting a second subprocess or telemetry provider throws the duplicate-service/duplicate-load error.
Registering two LSP providers for .ts fails with LSP_CONFLICT before any route is published.

recovery.scenario: Remove the duplicate provider row, restart the composition, and confirm the remaining provider serves the capability.

limitations: Seam-alone inertness is documented per package but not uniformly testable because some registries still publish a key.
Exclusive extension ownership is per runtime; a deployment-level selector is proposed only.
Same-process plugins can bypass registry APIs; exclusivity is not a security boundary.

mechanisms.title: Model-experience disclosure: what the model sees, token cost, and KV-cache effect
mechanisms.problem: A package can change the request prefix, add tool schemas, or inject history messages without the deployment noticing; undisclosed model input is both a cost surprise and a cache-invalidation surprise.
triggers: A package registers a tool, prompt section, runtime-context message, or session event that reaches the model
A package toggles tools or prompt text at runtime
Reviewing a package for prompt/cache impact
obligations: Every package README has a Model Experience section stating exactly what the model sees, or 'None' with the reason.
The section separates Token effect from KV Cache effect.
Direct effects (schemas, prompt sections, notices) and indirect effects (through a consumer package) are distinguished; the consumer that owns the request-prefix change is named.
Prefix-stable content is identified; append-only results are stated not to invalidate existing cache entries; a tool-list or prefix change states that reuse ends at the first changed token.

Packages with no model surface say so explicitly with the reason (for example browsing or workspace records never enter a model request); saying None is a disclosure, not a claim that the package registers no session events.
Truncation, spill replacement, and offload decisions that alter model-visible text are described, including whether the omission is permanent.

An image offload is permanent and model-visible: on `IMAGE_OFFLOAD_REQUIRED` with `offloadImages`, the plugin replaces the named images in request order with text placeholders naming each attachment and its read-only path, records the selection, retries without spending the provider retry budget, and keeps the omission across route changes, resume, and replay; provider cache reuse ends at the first changed message.
steps: Enumerate every model-visible artifact the package contributes.
Classify each as fixed per request, repeated until compaction, conditional, or none.
State cache behavior in terms of the request prefix and append-only history.
If the effect is owned by another package, link to that package and say so instead of duplicating its numbers.
Re-check the section when a tool is added or the package becomes enabled by default.

enforcement.implementation: Documentation review checks presence and specificity; no machine check proves the claimed token/cache behavior matches runtime.
enforcement.trust: Claims are advisory to deployments; the generated tool and configuration catalogs remain the authority for schemas and fields.
enforcement.failure: An omitted or wrong disclosure causes unexpected token spend or cache invalidation; it does not fail the build.
enforcement.exceptions: Pure library seams with no request contribution use the explicit None form; indirect contributions link to the owning consumer.

mechanisms.applicability: Every package that can be composed into an agent runtime. The section is still required when the answer is None.

migration.strategy: Add the section to the package template and audit existing packages by grepping for tool/prompt registration. Record the owner of each request-prefix change.
migration.implementation: A checklist in the README template plus a review rule: no package merge without Model Experience and Known Limitations sections.
migration.requiredSupport: Access to the runtime's prompt assembly and tool registry to verify what the package actually contributes.

positive.scenario: A package that registers a tool states its fixed schema cost and that the schema is prefix-stable while the tool view is unchanged.
A pure UI package states None and a runtime check confirms it registers no tool or prompt section.

rejection.scenario: A README without Model Experience fails the documentation checklist.
A package that injects a prompt section but claims None is rejected in review.

recovery.scenario: Add the missing section, classify the effect, and re-run the prompt-assembly diff to confirm the claim.

limitations: Token estimates are not exact for all providers.
Cache behavior can depend on the upstream provider and on route changes the package does not control.
The section is prose; nothing tests that a later code change keeps it true.

mechanisms.title: Known limitations, deferred work, and non-authoritative Dev Notes
mechanisms.problem: Without an explicit limits section, consumers infer guarantees the package does not provide (durability, security isolation, crash safety, cross-platform support) and build on them.
triggers: A package cannot meet a guarantee in some deployment (remote, headless, Windows, crash, multi-process)
A capability is deliberately out of scope or deferred
A maintainer records an undecided direction
obligations: Every package README carries Known Limitations and Deferred Work, phrased as current package constraints rather than a general comparison or a task backlog.
Each limitation states the operational condition, what still works, and the consequence.
Security, durability, and compatibility non-guarantees are listed explicitly (for example: file effects only, no reconnect/replay, process-local residency).
Deferred work is named as deferred, not promised; future behavior must not be described as shipped.
The Dev Note is explicitly non-authoritative maintainer context and must not carry new obligations.
steps: List the conditions under which the package is a poor fit.
For each, state the observable consequence and the reachable workaround if one exists.
Move genuinely undecided directions into a Dev Note labelled non-authoritative.
Remove limitations that no longer hold when the implementation changes; do not accumulate stale claims.

enforcement.implementation: Documentation review checks presence and honesty; no checker can prove completeness of a limitations list.
enforcement.trust: Limitations are the package's own risk disclosure; consuming deployments must verify the specific condition they rely on.
enforcement.failure: An unstated limitation becomes a production incident or an unsafe assumption.
enforcement.exceptions: None; even the smallest native addon README states platform support and failure behavior.

mechanisms.applicability: Every package README, including group maps and native-addon packages.

migration.strategy: Add the section to the template and require it in review. Split 'current constraint' from 'deferred work' so readers do not treat a future item as a guarantee.
migration.implementation: README checklist plus a review rule; for security-relevant packages, require the threat-model non-guarantees in the same section.
migration.requiredSupport: A glossary that distinguishes limitation, deferred work, and accepted residual risk.

positive.scenario: A sandbox package lists file-effects-only, denial inference, and fail-closed behavior in Known Limitations.
A Dev Note is labelled non-authoritative and points to the shipped sections for authority.

rejection.scenario: A README that promises reconnect/replay but the implementation document says no reconnect is rejected.
Deferred work described as available behavior is rejected in review.

recovery.scenario: Move the promised item back to Deferred Work and link the acceptance evidence required to ship it.

limitations: The completeness of a limitations list is a human judgement.
Some limits are discovered only by adversarial testing; the README is not a substitute for that test.

mechanisms.title: Configuration surface: declared fields, defaults, validation boundaries, and exhaustive catalogs
mechanisms.problem: Undocumented or loosely validated configuration produces deployments that boot with nonsensical limits, silently ignore fields, or fail at the first model request instead of at load.
triggers: Adding or changing a configuration field
Mounting a package in a new deployment
A settings form or generated catalog is generated from the schema
obligations: The package README lists the fields it accepts, or links the exhaustive generated catalog; a field table is a summary, not a second schema.
The generated configuration catalog is declared the exhaustive source for accepted fields and JSDoc; the README table is a summary, not a second schema.
Validation happens at a declared boundary: construction/load for impossible values, assembly/first call for values that depend on other plugins, and execution for request-time route checks.
Invalid values fail loudly; they must not be coerced into a plausible default.
Fields that cannot take effect until restart say so; fields resolved per request say so.
A field that is retired is declared as not read and not rewritten, rather than silently ignored.
Cap values with security meaning (URL length, redirects, image bytes, timeouts, frame sizes) are explicit and range-checked.

Prompt assembly exposes `includeHarnessIdentity`, `includeRuntimeContext`, `personaPrefix`, `personaSuffix`, and `toolOrder`. A `complete: true` section becomes the exact complete prompt after assembly (more than one effective complete section fails assembly), while assembled context/tools/variables remain separate inputs; an empty rendered prompt causes the loop to clear all effective system nodes. `toolOrder` shape errors fail at load, but an unknown tool name fails at the first assembly.
steps: Define the schema before documenting it.
Document required versus optional and the exact default.
State validation timing and the failure code or message.
Regenerate the configuration catalog and link it from the README.
Test one invalid value per validation boundary.

enforcement.implementation: Per-package schema validation runs at plugin construction or at the documented assembly/execution boundary; the generated catalog check keeps docs and schema aligned.
enforcement.trust: Schema validation is authoritative for shape and ranges; semantic serviceability checks (for example credential resolution or catalog model errors) may occur per request.
enforcement.failure: Load or assembly throws with the field and reason; the deployment must fix the value. A route that is configured-but-unserviceable may remain editable with a diagnostic.
enforcement.exceptions: Some fields intentionally accept omission to mean 'ambient provider discovery' or 'feature disabled'; this must be documented as the default.

mechanisms.applicability: Any package with a Config object, YAML row configuration, or user-facing settings form.

migration.strategy: Generate the catalog from the schema and make the README link it. Add validation-boundary tests before adding fields.
migration.implementation: A schema-to-catalog generator plus a CI diff check; per-package tests for load-time and assembly-time failures.
migration.requiredSupport: A configuration schema library and a generator that can render defaults and JSDoc.

positive.scenario: Every documented field appears in the generated catalog with the same default.
A negative or fractional spill budget fails plugin load.

rejection.scenario: An invalid timeout or a non-integer retry count is rejected at construction.
An unknown model route with no api/baseURL/models is refused where the profile is written.

recovery.scenario: Correct the field, reload the plugin, and confirm the catalog and effective value agree.

limitations: The README table can drift from the schema if the catalog check is not wired into CI.
Validation timing is package-specific; a value accepted at load can still fail at first call.
Some defaults depend on the deployment (OS temp directory, route catalog) and are described rather than fixed.

mechanisms.title: Settings persistence, precedence, reset, and legacy import
mechanisms.problem: Multiple configuration writers (profile patches, home patches, command-line overlays, forms, device-local storage) can silently overwrite each other or lose values across releases.
triggers: Editing live plugin configuration through a form
Shipping a new configuration layer or migrating an old settings file
Changing a preference schema or storage location
obligations: Forms expose only volatile fields from active, uniquely addressed profile entries; ordinary configuration stays in Cordis configuration files.
A form write persists through the active profile's Cordis patch and is refused if a home patch or command-line overlay would override it.
Reset restores the value beneath the profile override, including schema defaults; it cannot delete a value supplied by a lower layer.

Legacy settings are imported once after the Loader settles: the file is renamed before the first write, each section maps to a specific entry id, and a rejected section stays only in the renamed file.
A user override replaces the complete child list; it does not merge future builtin changes automatically.
Saved user overrides survive plugin unload while the command bindings themselves disappear with the owning plugin.
Preference stores declare their schema version and migrate on the next successful write; unreadable or future-version data is never replaced by reset.
内置 preset row（如 `preset-standard`）提供 `config.plugins` 默认；Web 编辑器保存的编辑按 plugin id 覆盖该 row 的对应插件，未编辑的 id 保留内置默认；row 级 patch replace 与 plugin 级用户覆盖是两层不同粒度。
steps: Declare config as volatile only when the live form is the intended editor.
Check precedence before writing; refuse writes that an overlay would shadow.
Implement reset as restoring the inherited layer, not deleting keys blindly.
Import legacy files behind an idempotent rename and log rejected sections.
Bump the preference schema version only when the next write can safely migrate.

enforcement.implementation: The settings service validates against the full plugin Config, rejects stale revisions, and compares the active override layers before persisting; import runs once after Loader settlement.
enforcement.trust: The active profile patch is the persistence authority; business plugins read their Config references directly, not the form projection.
enforcement.failure: A stale write is refused; an unreadable preference document disables edits until repaired; a rejected legacy section remains in the renamed file for manual handling.
enforcement.exceptions: Device-local stores (browser origin storage, Electron userData) are separate from Harness home and are not migrated by the settings service.

mechanisms.applicability: Deployments with layered configuration and a live settings UI. Command-line-only deployments can skip the form but still need precedence rules.

migration.strategy: Keep one persistence owner per layer, add an explicit precedence table, and migrate legacy files once with a rename-before-write protocol.
migration.implementation: Settings service with revisioned descriptors plus a legacy importer; tests for overlay refusal, reset, and idempotent import.
migration.requiredSupport: A config editor that can write the active profile patch and a home-path resolver.

positive.scenario: A form edit writes the profile patch and survives restart.
A legacy settings.yaml is imported once and renamed to settings.yaml.imported.

rejection.scenario: A form write shadowed by a home patch or CLI overlay is refused.
A stale revision edit is rejected instead of overwriting a newer value.

recovery.scenario: Remove the overriding layer or reset the field, then retry the edit.

limitations: Nested Includes own separate configurations and are not editable through the active profile form.
Cross-tab or cross-process writes can still be last-writer-wins at the storage layer.
A user override replacing a list does not receive later builtin additions.

mechanisms.title: Credential references, secret redaction, and repository-external secret files
mechanisms.problem: Secrets committed to configuration, echoed in logs, or resolved from ambient environment without an explicit reference leak across deployments and into support artifacts.
triggers: Adding a provider, backend, or publishing target that authenticates
Building a settings form that displays configuration
Recording errors or audit events around an authenticated operation
obligations: Configuration carries a reference (for example apiKeyEnv) or a store record id, never a plaintext secret.
Credential references resolve per request through the credential seam; a reference that resolves to nothing fails loudly with a stable missing-credential code.
Secret-role values are redacted from values, inherited values, profile overrides, and schema defaults; clients receive presence markers only.
Publishing credentials live outside Git in filesystem-permission-protected files; the CI uploader accepts permanent COS credentials, not STS session credentials.
Missing CI configuration stops publication; there is no personal-token fallback.
Anonymous fetch sends no credentials; SSH uses a deployment-owned alias and verifies artifact digests.
Error messages and audit records exclude credential values, authorization headers, and raw SDK errors.

Stored login records are addressable only by a lowercase-hyphenated provider id; a hand-declared route outside that grammar cannot be signed into because the record write fails `LlmError('UNSTORABLE_PROVIDER_ID')`, and such routes authenticate through `apiKeyEnv` or ambient provider settings. Omitting `apiKeyEnv` leaves a route configured-but-keyless, deferring to native ambient discovery for catalog routes.
steps: Add the credential to the credential store or the deployment's external file.
Reference it by name in configuration.
Resolve it at the operation boundary and fail with the documented code if absent.
Redact it from any form or log projection.
Verify the negative case (missing reference) without printing the secret.

enforcement.implementation: The credential seam resolves references; the settings form projection strips secret roles; the uploader validates configuration and skips credentials in child environments; audit records omit secrets.
enforcement.trust: A reference is only as trustworthy as the deployment's credential store. A provider that reads its own files may bypass the seam, and the README says so.
enforcement.failure: A missing or unusable reference fails the request (MISSING_CREDENTIAL/INVALID_CREDENTIAL) rather than falling back to an ambient secret.
enforcement.exceptions: Provider-native ambient discovery is allowed when a route names no credential; the README documents that this may read provider files outside the seam.

mechanisms.applicability: Every deployment that authenticates to a provider, remote host, object store, or update channel.

migration.strategy: Replace plaintext configuration values with references, back them with a credential store, and add negative tests for absent references.
migration.implementation: Credential seam plus a settings projection that redacts secret roles; CI configuration files kept outside the repository.
migration.requiredSupport: A credential store, per-request resolver, and log/audit redaction.

positive.scenario: A provider route with apiKeyEnv resolves the key per request and never writes it to config.
The settings form shows a presence marker for a secret field and no value.

rejection.scenario: A route whose apiKeyEnv resolves to nothing fails with MISSING_CREDENTIAL.
Publication without the required credential file stops instead of falling back to a personal token.

recovery.scenario: Add the external credential file or store record, retry, and confirm no secret appears in the log.

limitations: Provider-native discovery can read credential files the seam does not mediate.
A sign-in lives only in the process that started it; a reload abandons the pending authorization.
Headers supplied as plain strings can carry a credential the redactor never sees; the documented rule is to use a reference.

mechanisms.title: Optional and experimental bundles: off by default, enable/disable, caches, and model effects
mechanisms.problem: Experimental capability shipped in a profile can become active without an explicit user decision, can mutate tools or prompts at runtime, and can leave artifacts behind after being disabled.
triggers: Adding an experimental or optional bundle
Enabling or disabling a bundle from the Plugins UI
Overriding a bundle's rows from a later profile layer
obligations: Optional and experimental bundles are installed but disabled in shipped profiles; the README names the default state.
Enabling is an explicit user action in Plugins; the bundle patch inserts its rows, and disabling removes the profile layer.
A later profile patch may override or disable a bundle by row id, but an override alone does not select the bundle.
Disabling removes tools/UI contributions; existing checkouts and branches remain (tool-worktree), and some bundles install native runtime even while disabled (voice-input).
Toggling a bundle that changes the tool list or prompt invalidates the cached request prefix once; the README states that effect.
A bundle that adds no model tool says so, and a bundle that adds one states its schema cost and completion behavior.
Enabling or disabling changes the running Host tool list, so every Agent sees the change on its next request in every preset, including minimal.

A bundle that replaces the title provider states the switch scope and failure retention: session-titles replaces the first-prompt title provider for existing and new Sessions, preserves user-pinned titles, keeps the previous title on failure, includes the current generated title in its 4096-byte title-input budget, and rejects oversized input instead of truncating conversation history.
steps: Write cordis.patch.yml rows that are inert until selected.
Document the exact default (on/off) and the enable/disable path.
State what deletion removes and what persists.
State the model-visible delta and cache effect.
Verify that disable leaves the base composition valid.

enforcement.implementation: Profile patch selection: shipped profiles omit the bundle row; enabling adds the layer and disabling removes it. Profile composer owns patch ordering and errors.
enforcement.trust: A user or profile editor controls selection; a later patch can still override rows, and the README states that this does not count as selection.
enforcement.failure: Removing a row unregisters its tools/UI; a component that fails to deactivate is a composition error rather than a partial enable.
enforcement.exceptions: Features enabled by the base bundle (for example automatic compaction) are documented as default-on rather than optional.

mechanisms.applicability: Any feature whose default activation would change model input, spend external resources, download assets, or modify the workspace.

migration.strategy: Keep the capability implementation in a normal package and put only composition rows in the bundle. Add the bundle disabled by default and document the switch.
migration.implementation: cordis.patch.yml plus a plugin-manager entry; tests that enable, disable, and re-enable without duplicating registrations.
migration.requiredSupport: A profile composer that can insert/remove layers and report errors; a plugin inventory projection.

positive.scenario: A fresh profile has the bundle row absent and the tool/UI absent.
Enabling the bundle registers its tool once; disabling removes it without deleting existing checkouts or branches.

rejection.scenario: A profile override of a bundle row that does not select the bundle leaves the feature off.
A second provider registered by enabling the bundle fails the duplicate-service check.

recovery.scenario: Disable the bundle, confirm the tool/UI disappears on the next request, then remove residual assets separately if required.

limitations: Disabling cannot undo durable effects such as generated titles or created worktrees.
Some bundles install native dependencies even while disabled; the disk/download cost remains.
Browser-half packages can suspend waiting for a page even when the profile is otherwise headless.

mechanisms.title: Model-facing tool results: bounded output, stable codes, caller-derived authority, no hidden cursors
mechanisms.problem: Tool output that is unbounded, ambiguous, or grants authority based on model-supplied identifiers can exhaust context, hide failures, or let a model read another workspace's data.
triggers: Adding or changing a model-facing tool
A tool returns large output, paginated results, or cross-session data
A tool result is rendered by a generic spill or presentation layer
obligations: Results are bounded through documented caps, paging footers, or the shared spill policy; custom compositions without that policy can receive complete inline payloads (session query states this).
Failures use stable machine-routable codes plus a recovery instruction; callers must not parse prose.
Search/query results are cursor-free: no provider cursor, offset, page size, or model-controlled limit reaches the model; a capped result asks the model to narrow the query.
Authority is derived from the caller (Agent/Session identity), never from a model-supplied id; cross-session access requires exact workspace equality and unauthorized boundaries carry no hidden ids.
Successful results use the documented envelope; read results use line-numbered content with an exact footer; write/edit return a compact confirmation while arguments retain the full text.
A generic spill policy owns truncation/recovery; an individual tool must not invent a second truncation format.
Tool names and field names stay compatible with the existing schema vocabulary (snake_case, canonical names); renaming a tool changes its category and must be documented.

Filesystem mutations are gated by an observation policy rather than tool-local state: writing/editing an unread target fails `FS_NOT_OBSERVED`, a changed file fails `FS_STALE_VERSION` with a re-read instruction, successful reads emit `fs/observed`, and observation listeners must be synchronous side-effect-only recorders (a later mutation rechecks under the target lock).
steps: Define the result envelope and error codes before the executor.
Resolve the caller identity and workspace from execution context, not arguments.
Bound output and add the exact continuation/recovery text.
Route oversized output through the shared spill policy.
Test the unauthorized case and the at-cap case.

enforcement.implementation: Executors enforce caps and authorization in trusted code; the shared spill policy replaces oversized accepted content after tool post-execute; stable error constructors normalize messages.
enforcement.trust: The tool boundary is trusted only for the caller identity the host supplies. A local argument-validation error keeps its own message; trusted service failures are sanitized.
enforcement.failure: A denied or invalid call returns an error result the model can read; an oversized result is spilled or capped rather than sent whole; a missing capability refuses execution.
enforcement.exceptions: A custom composition without the spill policy accepts complete payloads inline; the package README states that consequence.

mechanisms.applicability: All model-facing tools, especially those returning files, search results, session history, or command output.

migration.strategy: Introduce a shared result envelope, stable error codes, and one spill policy; migrate tools one at a time and keep old tool names working until callers update.
migration.implementation: Tool executor helpers for caps/envelopes plus a post-execute retention policy; authorization helpers that read execution context.
migration.requiredSupport: A tool registry with execution context, a token meter, and a spill store.

positive.scenario: A read over the cap returns the exact footer and the next offset.
A session query for another workspace returns SESSION_QUERY_TOOL_UNAUTHORIZED without leaking ids.

rejection.scenario: A model-supplied limit or cursor is rejected as an unknown argument.
A write without a prior read returns FS_NOT_OBSERVED with the read-then-retry instruction.

recovery.scenario: Read the file, retry the write, and confirm the stale-version path returns FS_STALE_VERSION with re-read guidance.

limitations: Caps are estimates for token cost; provider-reported usage remains authoritative.
Spill notices are a text convention and cannot prove the policy saved the result.
A same-process tool can still return data the model should not see if the host supplies the wrong caller identity.

mechanisms.title: Fail-closed enforcement: no silent downgrade to unconfined or unverified operation
mechanisms.problem: When an enforcement component is missing or fails, the convenient behavior is to continue without it. That silently converts a confined operation into an unconfined one or a verified artifact into an unverified one.
triggers: A confined mode is requested but no runner can enforce it
An installed helper, digest, protocol, or platform does not match
A security-relevant path is symlinked, writable by others, or outside the allowed root
Required publishing or tagging configuration is absent
obligations: A confined mode with no usable runner rejects with a stable unavailable code (SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE); unconfined passthrough never happens for a confined policy.
A runner failure outranks a denial and is reported as a sandbox problem, not a command failure.
Digest, protocol-version, runtime-kind, and platform/architecture mismatches are rejected before readiness, not repaired by fallback.
A hostname answer set containing any non-public address is rejected in full; the connection is pinned to the validated set; cross-origin redirects fail.
Spill writes use exclusive create with owner-only permissions and refuse symlinks or pre-existing targets.
Missing publication configuration, debugging artifacts, or required signatures stop the operation; there is no personal-token fallback.
A denial is a structured result (FS_SANDBOX_DENIED or sandbox denial marker), not stderr inference where the fence owns the decision.

Every Gateway invocation and stream names an explicit Peer; a disposed Peer fails with `gateway/peer-disposed` before the payload is read. For a non-owner principal, resources are resolved from type-validated arguments and `ctx.remoteAccess.decide({principal, action, resources, args})` runs after input validation but before lookup, Context resolution, or Session activation; a denial throws `remote-access/denied` and an invalid resource is refused with `resource-invalid` without asking. Owner calls bypass the decision. `$events` and `$events/result` require `peer.interactions === 'answer'`; buffered uplink above `streamInboxBytes` fails the stream with `gateway/uplink-overflow` without closing the socket.
steps: Identify every path where the enforcement component can be absent.
Return a stable unavailable/denied code instead of running the operation.
Preserve enough evidence to distinguish runner failure from operation failure.
Add a test that removes the runner and asserts the rejection.
Document the one approved recovery path (fix the runner or explicitly choose an unconfined executor).

enforcement.implementation: Bash executor checks ctx.sandbox.confine() and rejects SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE; fs fence re-canonicalizes and returns FS_SANDBOX_DENIED; SSH validates digests/protocol; web fetch rejects non-public answers; publish workflows fail when configuration or evidence is missing.
enforcement.trust: These are trusted-code checks, not kernel boundaries. They prevent accidental downgrade, not a hostile process with equivalent privileges.
enforcement.failure: The operation fails closed with a code and, where applicable, a runner-failure fact or audit stage; the caller may retry only after fixing the environment.
enforcement.exceptions: danger-full-access explicitly bypasses the sandbox and is stamped as unconfined; that is a chosen mode, not a silent fallback.

mechanisms.applicability: Security-relevant executors, remote transports, publishers, and any component whose absence changes the guarantee.

migration.strategy: Enumerate enforcement points, define unavailable codes, and make absence a hard error. Add negative tests before enabling the feature by default.
migration.implementation: Error types per component plus tests that remove the runner/digest/config and assert rejection.
migration.requiredSupport: A composition that can omit the provider in tests and a stable error taxonomy.

positive.scenario: A confined bash call runs with the selected mode and reports enforcement facts.
A public web fetch resolves, pins, and returns a capped body.

rejection.scenario: Removing the sandbox runner makes the same bash call fail SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE.
A helper digest mismatch prevents SSH readiness.

recovery.scenario: Restore the runner or helper, re-run the operation, and verify the mode/enforcement facts before relying on the result.

limitations: Fail-closed cannot detect a compromised runner that reports success.
Denials inferred from stderr in bash can misclassify application errors or miss a denial outside the retained tail.
Publication approval gates the workflow, not arbitrary code under the same machine account.

mechanisms.title: Trust-boundary declaration and residual risk
mechanisms.problem: A component named 'sandbox', 'scope', or 'approval' invites consumers to treat it as a security boundary. When it is a policy fence, a cooperative primitive, or an approval gate over one workflow, over-trusting it defeats the actual protection.
triggers: A package uses the words sandbox, isolation, scope, trust, or approval
A deployment composes a security-sensitive capability
Reviewing a security claim in a package README
obligations: State what the boundary does NOT protect: fs-sandbox is a policy fence over a model-controlled path, not a kernel boundary; the residual resolve-to-syscall TOCTOU is narrowed but accepted.
The dynamic Cordis vm isolates globals but is not a security boundary; its services reach the live runtime, so treat a dynamic package like bash access.

Scoped registration routes trusted same-process plugins and is not a sandbox or authority boundary: state isolation applies only to scope-aware APIs and events, an arbitrary Cordis service remains context-global when called through a scoped context, one context carries one nearest scope key, and handing out `Scope.ctx` hands out the minting plugin's injected services.

Iframe sandboxing trades compatibility for isolation; escaped popups retain an opener, cross-origin pages can still navigate at the top level after the sandbox is disabled, and private-network filtering is not a firewall.

SSH digest verification detects an unexpected installed artifact but does not make writable deployment files safe to execute; TLS stream keys do not protect against remote process-memory inspection, and no reconnect or replay is supplied.
An approval environment gates the workflow, not arbitrary code running under the same machine account; account isolation and source-branch restrictions are separate work.
Subagent requests/results are borrowed trusted same-process values; serialization and hostile-input validation belong at process and wire boundaries.

Instruction candidates whose final path component is a symlink are resolved across the trust boundary: a cloned repository can surface off-tree content as lower-authority workspace guidance (never overriding system, developer, or direct user instructions), so loading an untrusted repository requires a filesystem policy gate or OS sandbox around `ctx.fs`.

Child processes receive a scrubbed environment: credential-shaped names and ambient `DSH_*` facts are removed before the caller explicit `env` merges, an explicit `undefined` tombstone removes an ordinary entry, and `argv` is never shell-interpreted; transports that own their spawn import `scrubbedParentEnv` so environment policy remains single-sourced.

An SDK stdio profile keeps stdout protocol-only (newline-delimited JSON-RPC); arbitrary inserted user plugins cannot be constrained by the shipped bundle, a custom profile must retain the `dsh-sdk-jsonrpc-server` row, and disabling HMR means configuration changes require a restart.
steps: Write the threat model in one paragraph: what is untrusted, what is trusted, what is out of scope.
Name the residual risk and why it is accepted.
Name the component that owns kernel-grade or cross-process isolation instead.
Prevent stronger claims in the README and in UI copy.

enforcement.implementation: Human security review and documentation review; no runtime check proves a threat model.
enforcement.trust: The declaration is only as good as the reviewer. Tests demonstrate specific behaviors, not the absence of all escapes.
enforcement.failure: An overstated guarantee leads to unsafe composition; the mitigation is correction and, where possible, a compensating control at a higher layer.
enforcement.exceptions: A deployment may add a stronger boundary (OS sandbox, separate account, network policy) outside the package; the README should point to where that belongs.

mechanisms.applicability: Any component whose name or API implies confinement, isolation, authorization, or approval.

migration.strategy: Add a mandatory threat-model/non-guarantee paragraph to security-adjacent READMEs and review UI copy for stronger language.
migration.implementation: A README checklist question: 'What does this not protect against, and who owns that protection?'
migration.requiredSupport: A security review process and a place to record accepted residual risk.

positive.scenario: fs-sandbox documentation states policy-fence status and the accepted TOCTOU residual risk.
The Cordis runner documentation states the vm is not a security boundary and compares the package to bash access.

rejection.scenario: A README claiming kernel-grade isolation for the fs fence is rejected.
An approval claim that covers arbitrary account code is rejected unless account isolation exists.

recovery.scenario: Correct the claim, add the residual-risk paragraph, and link the component that owns the stronger boundary.

limitations: Threat models age; a later change can invalidate the stated assumptions.
Review cannot prove the absence of an escape; adversarial testing and external audit remain necessary for high-assurance use.

mechanisms.title: Registration lifetime, scope isolation, and atomic contributions
mechanisms.problem: Registrations that outlive their owner leak across agents and reloads; registrations that commit partially leave a registry in a state no one can reason about; scope filters that do not match ownership let a contribution be visible in one scope and torn down by another.
triggers: Registering a tool, prompt section, command, extension, provider, projection, or module
Unloading or replacing a plugin
Creating per-agent or per-group registries
obligations: Registration runs through a scoped context or a Cordis effect; the disposer withdraws exactly that contribution.
A contribution is atomic: validate package-face identity, schemas, and invocation descriptors before committing; duplicates reject the whole batch before any state changes.
A registration made through a scoped context is both scope-visible and scope-lifetime; do not make something visible in one scope but owned by another.
Child scopes inherit ancestor contributions with nearest definition precedence; ancestor listeners may observe descendants, never the reverse; disposing a scope removes everything it owns.
Registrations that are effects disappear when the mounting fiber unloads; an absent registry makes the unit inert rather than partially registered.
Merge-extensible vocabulary (capability kinds, resource kinds, activity kinds) is declaration-merged by the owner; existing entries keep registration order.
A registry change is published to subscribers; a throwing listener is logged and does not stop later listeners.

Subagent delegation capacity is a tree-wide pool: `maxActiveSubagents` defaults to 8, the root parent consumes no slot, creation/cold resume reserves before yielding, waiting/pending-inbox/stopping activations stay counted, admission never queues, lowering the limit refuses new admissions without evicting residents, and slots are process-local. At capacity, creation rejects `ACTIVATION_LIMIT_REACHED` (browser prompts get `subagent/delivery-unavailable`).

Command registration rejects duplicate ids and overlapping default key combinations across the supported device profiles; fixed read-only sequences participate in conflict checks, cannot be assigned to editable commands, and remain visible-but-non-executable when a saved binding collides with a mounted fixed action.
steps: Mint or receive the scope that matches the intended lifetime.
Validate the complete contribution before writing any state.
Register through one effect and keep the returned disposer.
For scoped data, file by scopeOf() and dispatch through scopeTarget(); do not rely on a scoped context alone.
Test unload and duplicate cases.

enforcement.implementation: Cordis effect ownership and scoped stores; typert's atomic register with duplicate rejection; LSP effect-scoped provider routes; client entry ownership and stale-factory discard.
enforcement.trust: The registry trusts same-process callers to use the API; it prevents lifecycle leaks and accidental duplicates, not malicious mutation.
enforcement.failure: A duplicate rejects before commit; a disposed scope removes its registrations; a late or stale module download cannot mount after its desired entry changed.
enforcement.exceptions: Some saved user data (keybinding overrides, preset selections) intentionally outlives the contributing plugin; the README states that.

mechanisms.applicability: Any registry, extension point, event surface, or scoped service in a plugin architecture.

migration.strategy: Move registration into effects, add a scope primitive for per-agent isolation, and make registration validation atomic.
migration.implementation: A scope store with createScope/scopeTarget/ScopedLayers plus registry-level duplicate checks and disposer tests.
migration.requiredSupport: A plugin container with effect ownership and a way to mint scoped contexts.

positive.scenario: Unloading a plugin removes its tool and prompt registration; re-loading registers one instance.
A tool registered through agent.ctx is visible only to that agent.

rejection.scenario: Registering a duplicate typert contribution rejects the whole batch and leaves the registry unchanged.
A second LSP provider for the same extension fails before publishing a route.

recovery.scenario: Remove the duplicate or dispose the previous scope, then re-register and verify the registry change event.

limitations: Only scope-aware APIs isolate state; an arbitrary service called through a scoped context remains context-global.
A context carries one nearest scope key; multi-membership policy sets are unsupported.
Service reachability comes from the scope minter and cannot be narrowed later by the holder.

mechanisms.title: Durability and restart semantics: durable, process-local, and interrupted states
mechanisms.problem: Consumers assume state survives a restart when it is process-local, or assume a restart is clean when a write was interrupted. Both errors produce lost work, duplicate side effects, or broken indexes.
triggers: Storing state that consumers expect to read after restart
Writing multiple records that must agree
Resuming a session, child agent, or restored cache
Publishing a multi-object operation
obligations: Each package declares its state class: durable domain records, persisted caches, process-local registries, or in-memory projections.
Restored rows are schema-validated; a corrupt row is discarded rather than seeding a broken fold.
Multi-write mutations use an explicit pending marker so startup completes or rolls back exactly the interrupted operation.
A cold resume states its prerequisites (persistence, session query, preset definition) and rejects with a stable code when they are missing.
Process-local definitions disappear on restart; historical logs retain arguments and receipts but do not restore the registry.
A client applies only the Host release it booted from; another release's modules stay outside the queue until the Host returns.
Telemetry/audit cursors mean handed-off, not delivered; a missing terminal result means interruption, not success.
One-shot cleanup runs at activation and does not sweep again until restart; the README states that retention is not continuous.

A projection unit is a pure fold over committed session events; its wire value is whole-value (the complete array, strictly increasing by turn) so consumers replace and never merge, and a draft-only change must not advance the public value. Restored cached rows are schema-validated, including ordering, and corrupt rows are discarded instead of feeding a broken fold.

Archive admission is a capability seam: `workspace/session-activity` asks composed providers what still runs and `WorkspaceActiveSessionError` refuses a non-empty answer; `stopActivity: true` persists the archive before dispatching the parallel stop so the durable set blocks wakeups, and provider stop errors are logged while the archive survives. Removing a project never deletes its folder, files, or session histories.
steps: Classify the state and write the classification down.
Persist a mutation marker before the records can diverge.
Validate on restore and define the discard behavior.
Document the resume prerequisites and the failure code.
Test crash points: before marker, after first write, after commit, during cleanup.

enforcement.implementation: Workspace pendingMutation and startup validation; turn-outline persisted schema validation; subagent cold-resume checks; client release equality gate; publish audit records and lock directories.
enforcement.trust: Durability is bounded by the storage backend and the process's ability to finish the recovery path; a crash between external side effects may still need manual reconciliation.
enforcement.failure: Corrupt state is discarded or fails loud as corruption; a missing terminal record is treated as interruption; an unrecoverable lock requires verifying no writer before manual removal.
enforcement.exceptions: A failed local agent without a committed turn/end settles as error; a later committed turn ending supplies the recovered outcome.

mechanisms.applicability: Packages with persistent stores, session-derived projections, resumable agents, publish/upload pipelines, and caches.

migration.strategy: Write an explicit state-class table per package, add a mutation marker for multi-write operations, and validate on every restore.
migration.implementation: Domain store with marker + startup recovery; schema-validated cache restore; resume tests with a missing prerequisite.
migration.requiredSupport: A durable storage backend, a schema validator, and a test harness that can simulate interruption.

positive.scenario: A workspace create/delete interrupted between writes is completed or rolled back on next startup.
A persisted turn-outline row with a non-increasing turn is discarded on restore.

rejection.scenario: Cold-resuming a child without persistence rejects with the documented continuation code.
A client receiving a graph from another Host release applies nothing and publishes a releaseChange event.

recovery.scenario: Remove the stale lock only after proving no writer, restore the failed operation from its audit record, and verify the terminal result exists.

limitations: A durable store does not make external side effects transactional.
Crash-loss windows remain in best-effort queues and one-shot cleanup.
Cross-process access to one persistence store is out of scope for several packages.

mechanisms.title: Generated artifacts, drift gates, and retained verification evidence
mechanisms.problem: Generated metadata, patches, and long-running diagnostics go stale silently. A green build or a cached install can then hide a generator mismatch, an unapplied patch, or a regression corpus that no longer represents the input space.
triggers: Changing a dependency that a generator reads
Changing a generator, patch, or generated file
Running (or deciding not to run) a diagnostic campaign
Publishing built artifacts
obligations: Generated files carry an owner and a regeneration command; they are never edited by hand.
A verify command recomputes the expected artifact from the installed dependency and current generator; a pre-commit check compares the staged generated file and CI verifies against the lockfile.
A dependency or generator change is staged together with the regenerated file; generation errors block the commit.
Patches to published packages are maintained with the package manager's patch workflow, exclude generated launchers, and are validated in a fresh extraction before relying on cached tests.
Long-running fuzz/diagnostic campaigns are explicit, not part of the default suite; failures are retained and exit nonzero; reports include input hash, whether it opened, and worktree status.
Baseline comparisons state their limits (current dependency versions, current helpers, no shipped browser profile) instead of claiming a full historical reproduction.
Retained fixtures are committed for unit/browser tests so those tests do not require the generator's runtime.
steps: Generate; review the diff; stage the generated file with the input change.
Run the verify/check command locally and in CI.
For patches, re-extract the dependency and verify patch application.
For diagnostics, keep corpus and reports, and state what the run does not prove.
Record the exact command, seed, versions, and result status.

enforcement.implementation: Pre-commit gen-provider-data --check --cached, CI verify-provider-data, generated diff review, fuzz runner exit status, publish hash/signature verification.
enforcement.trust: The generated artifact is authoritative only for the installed dependency and generator version; floating dependency drift can invalidate it until regeneration.
enforcement.failure: A stale generated file fails the check; a failed patch application fails the build/test; a fuzz defect exits nonzero even when the value difference is 'known'.
enforcement.exceptions: Unrequested prior-generation source maps may read the current map file; accepted damaged ZIP inputs are informational and need separate inspection.

mechanisms.applicability: Any repository with code generation, patched dependencies, binary fixtures, or long-running diagnostic campaigns.

migration.strategy: Add a generator owner marker and a verify command; wire the check into pre-commit and CI; move exploratory campaigns out of the default suite and commit representative fixtures.
migration.implementation: Generator script with --check mode, a pre-commit hook over relevant inputs, CI step, and a fixtures directory.
migration.requiredSupport: Deterministic generation, a lockfile, and a runner that records inputs and exit status.

positive.scenario: Updating the provider dependency and regenerating leaves the verify command green with the staged generated file.
A fuzz campaign with a known defect exits nonzero and retains the report.

rejection.scenario: Staging a hand-edited generated file fails the pre-commit check.
A patch that includes generated launchers is rejected in review.

recovery.scenario: Rerun the documented generation commands, stage both input and output, and retry the commit.

limitations: A generation probe covers installed resolvers, not all value-dependent branches.
Metadata-only revisions cannot distinguish content changes invisible in mtime/ctime/size.
A passing check proves agreement with the current generator, not semantic correctness of the generated content.

mechanisms.title: Version compatibility, legacy inputs, and explicit migration
mechanisms.problem: A format or preference change can break old deployments, silently rewrite user data, or leave two protocol peers unable to detect that they disagree.
triggers: Changing a persisted format, preference schema, wire protocol, or tool schema
Renaming or retiring a configuration field
Connecting components built at different versions
obligations: Legacy values are accepted and mapped at read time without rewriting the source (for example normal/expanded map to detailed; version 1 keybindings are read without rewrite).
A preference store declares its schema version and migrates on the next successful write; unreadable or future-version data is never replaced by reset.
A retired configuration field is declared as not read and not rewritten instead of being silently honored.
Wire peers reject mismatched protocol versions, runtime kinds, or digests before readiness.
Client module graphs carry a release identity (version plus commit); a page applies only its boot release and reports a release change.
Persisted records carry a version; old read shapes remain readable, and schema validation rejects unknown/corrupt shapes explicitly.
Renaming a tool or field is a compatibility change: snake_case and canonical names are preserved where external callers depend on them, and a rename changes presentation categories.
steps: Write the old and new shapes and the read-time mapping.
Version the persisted record or protocol.
Keep old readers working until the migration is complete; do not silently rewrite.
Add a negative test for a version mismatch.
Document the upgrade path and what cannot be migrated.

enforcement.implementation: Versioned schemas and protocol checks; legacy mapping in the reader; release equality gate; digest and kind checks at connection time.
enforcement.trust: Compatibility is best effort where an old artifact is genuinely unavailable; the README states which old records are accepted.
enforcement.failure: A mismatched protocol fails loudly; a corrupt row is discarded; an unreadable preference document disables edits rather than being overwritten.
enforcement.exceptions: Historical logs may be readable without being restorable (for example dynamic definitions); the README distinguishes the two.

mechanisms.applicability: Any package with persisted state, a wire protocol, external tool schemas, or user preferences.

migration.strategy: Version every persisted shape and wire message; add read-time legacy mapping; keep one write version at a time and test both sides of the boundary.
migration.implementation: Schema version fields plus migration-on-write; protocol version checks; compatibility tests with old fixtures.
migration.requiredSupport: Old fixtures, a version field, and a documented upgrade command.

positive.scenario: A version 1 keybinding file is read without rewrite and saved as version 2 on the next edit.
Legacy normal/expanded values display as detailed without rewriting the saved value.

rejection.scenario: A client with a mismatched release does not apply the other Host's graph.
An SSH helper with a mismatched protocol version or digest is refused before readiness.

recovery.scenario: Reconnect with matching versions, or run the documented migration, then verify the new value is readable.

limitations: Some historical artifacts are readable but not restorable.
A migration that requires an unavailable old definition is rejected rather than falling back.
Compatibility shims can accumulate; the README should name when they can be removed.

mechanisms.title: Outbound data disclosure: telemetry, external services, and what never reaches the model
mechanisms.problem: Session text, reasoning, file contents, and command output can leave the process through telemetry, translation, browsing, or fetch without a deployment realizing which copy is exported and whether it was redacted.
triggers: Mounting a telemetry backend
Sending reasoning or conversation text to an external service
Opening untrusted web content in an embedded browser
Fetching a public URL
obligations: State what leaves the process and to whom; a no-op or absent backend must not be described as delivery.
The canonical session log is never rewritten by redaction; redaction applies only to the outbound copy.
Every outbound record passes the redaction waterfall; with no rules mounted, records leave exactly as captured, and a throwing listener withholds that record fail-closed.
The backend discloses its sharing mode (full, feedback-only, disabled); this is a mode declaration, not a per-session receipt.
Delivery is best-effort: the cursor means handed-off, not delivered, and queued records may be lost on crash.
Feedback is a signal about output, never input to the model; per-message ratings survive restart but never enter model history or telemetry.
External reasoning translation discloses that displayed reasoning may contain private code or conversation details; requests never fall back to another provider.
Anonymous fetch sends no credentials; SSH aliases, authentication, and stream capabilities are private deployment details.
steps: Enumerate every outbound channel and its payload.
Mount redaction rules for each shared-collector deployment.
Verify the fail-closed behavior with a throwing listener.
Verify that the canonical log and model history are unchanged.
Document the loss window and deduplication key.

enforcement.implementation: Telemetry redaction waterfall and outbound-copy isolation; feedback storage separate from model history; browser protocol policy; anonymous fetch transport; credential/SSH private fields.
enforcement.trust: Redaction is only as good as the mounted rules; the package ships none. The backend SDK owns batching, retry, and loss.
enforcement.failure: A throwing redaction listener withholds that record; an unavailable external service fails the translation without fallback; a non-public fetch target is rejected.
enforcement.exceptions: A deployment that exports to a trusted collector may intentionally mount no rules; the README states that records then leave unchanged.

mechanisms.applicability: Deployments that export telemetry, call external services with user content, embed web pages, or fetch URLs.

migration.strategy: Inventory outbound channels, default to no export, and require explicit redaction rules before sending to a shared collector.
migration.implementation: One coordinator with a redaction waterfall and an outbound copy; per-channel documentation and tests.
migration.requiredSupport: A backend contract with emit/flush/shutdown, a redaction hook, and a deduplication key.

positive.scenario: A mounted telemetry backend receives records in order and the canonical session log is unchanged.
A translation request discloses the external service and keeps the original reasoning in the session.

rejection.scenario: A throwing redaction listener withholds that record instead of exporting it unredacted.
A fetch to a non-public address is rejected before response bytes are accepted.

recovery.scenario: Fix the redaction listener or remove it deliberately, then replay the unhanded records from the cursor.

limitations: No built-in redaction rules; exported data is as clean as the deployment's rules.
Best-effort delivery can lose queued records on crash.
On-demand redaction uses the policy mounted at capture time, not the policy at event time.

mechanisms.title: Human approval gates and the limits of local evidence
mechanisms.problem: Irreversible or privileged operations (publication, permission escalation, loading dynamic code into the live runtime) can be triggered by automation or by a model. Without an explicit human gate and an honest statement of what local checks prove, the operation looks approved when it is only technically possible.
triggers: Publishing or promoting an artifact to production
Escalating a sandbox mode
Loading a dynamic package with a browser half
Running a model-requested operation that needs wider permissions
obligations: Publication requires explicit operator authorization and GitHub Environment approval; test and production are separate environments with their own reviewers.
Only production creates the release tag; the App token is short-lived, and missing configuration stops publication with no personal-token fallback.
A debugging/unsigned package cannot publish; eligibility requires a new signed/notarized package, not a retry.
A denied sandbox operation may be retried once at the narrowest wider mode only after the approval prompt is accepted; nothing executes before approval.
A browser-half dynamic package waits for a page verdict; the run suspends until approved or cancelled, and there is no timeout.

State what local evidence does not prove: local fixtures do not establish COS/CDN/admin permissions; a successful run does not mean the UI rendered; approval gates the workflow, not arbitrary code under the same account.
Retain the approval summary, operation identity, events, and terminal result; a missing result means interruption, not success.
steps: Prepare the operation and its evidence.
Request approval with the exact version, channel, target, and hashes.
Execute only after approval; record the identity and outcome.
On failure, recover the exact prepared attempt or start a new authorized operation; do not rebuild merely to retry an upload.
State the evidence limits in the completion report.

enforcement.implementation: GitHub Environment required reviewers and allowed deployment branch; publisher rechecks signatures/hashes and refuses missing configuration; tool layer drives sandbox escalation; cordis runner suspends on a page verdict.
enforcement.trust: Approval is a human gate over a specific workflow. It does not isolate the machine account, and it does not prove external permissions.
enforcement.failure: A missing approval/configuration stops the operation; a rejected escalation leaves the original denial; a suspended run waits until cancelled.
enforcement.exceptions: Test environments may allow self-approval; developers still cannot skip a signed/notarized requirement for publishable artifacts.

mechanisms.applicability: Irreversible writes, production publication, privilege escalation, and dynamic code loading.

migration.strategy: Put irreversible operations behind an explicit approval environment and record the exact artifact identity; keep a preview/dry-run path.
migration.implementation: CI environments with required reviewers; a publish plan with hashes and signatures; an audit record with before/after state.
migration.requiredSupport: A CI provider with environment approvals, an artifact identity store, and a signed/notarized build pipeline.

positive.scenario: A production publish waits for the desktop-production environment approval and records the prepared identity.
A denied bash command offers exactly one wider-mode retry after user approval.

rejection.scenario: Publishing an unsigned or unnotarized package is rejected before upload.
Loading a browser-half dynamic package without a connected page leaves the run suspended, not silently succeeded.

recovery.scenario: Rebuild and sign a new package or restore the exact approved artifact, obtain a new approval, and verify the terminal audit result.

limitations: Approval reviewers may not understand the artifact; the gate does not replace technical verification.
A suspended run has no timeout and can block unattended automation.
Local checks cannot prove remote permissions or CDN behavior.

mechanisms.title: Packaging payloads and supply-chain identity
mechanisms.problem: A packaged runtime can accidentally include development artifacts, download at import time, or publish a payload for the wrong platform, producing a wheel/artifact that installs but cannot run or that silently mutates the environment.
triggers: Building a platform wheel, native addon package, or prebuilt runtime
Adding an optional download or payload directory
Publishing a client bundle
obligations: Published targets are explicit; the wheel tag and payload must match exactly, and unsupported targets are not published.
The package publishes wheels only and installs a command plus module; importing modules, starting profiles, or processing files never downloads resources.
Downloads are explicit API calls that verify archive hashes and package identities, preserve executable permissions, and publish completed directories atomically; failed downloads can be retried.
Resource identity includes the release's locked inputs; cache layout is documented, and unused versions require manual removal.
A dev-only carrier (for example runtime/node) is never selected automatically and is excluded from wheels and sdists.
Native platform packages carry binaries, use compatible dependency ranges, and reject missing/unloadable bindings without installation-time compilation; C sources ship for auditability.

A workspace-dependency payload has a validated manifest (platform/arch must match the process), a stable layout, and either in-place use or a copied installation; invalid payloads fail the first tool call.
Client bundles are built before launch; a missing bundle fails activation with one build instruction and the package/path list.
steps: Declare the published target matrix and the payload manifest.
Verify the tag/arch against the payload at build time.
Make downloads explicit and hash-verified; keep import paths download-free.
Exclude development carriers and source trees from the published artifact.
Test installation in a clean environment outside the checkout.

enforcement.implementation: Platform package metadata and wheel tags; payload manifest validation; download hash/identity verification; atomic cache publication; build guards excluding dev carriers.
enforcement.trust: The artifact is trusted only for the platform and locked inputs it declares; a floating dependency or hand-built payload is outside the guarantee.
enforcement.failure: A tag/payload mismatch, missing executable, or wrong platform rejects with a build/install instruction; a bad download fails and can be retried.
enforcement.exceptions: Unused workspace patches are permitted for packages outside the runtime closure during production deployment; repository installation still rejects unused patches.

mechanisms.applicability: Repositories that publish platform wheels, native addons, bundled runtimes, or prebuilt client assets.

migration.strategy: Split build-time and download-time resources, declare the target matrix, and add a clean-environment install smoke.
migration.implementation: Manifest-driven packaging with hash verification and atomic cache; CI matrix per target; installed-wheel smoke outside the checkout.
migration.requiredSupport: A release pipeline with per-target runners, a lockfile for payload inputs, and a cache directory policy.

positive.scenario: A wheel installs the command and module, and importing the module performs no download.
An external payload with the matching platform/arch manifest is used in place and returns the expected paths.

rejection.scenario: A wheel tag that does not match the payload is rejected at build/install.
A payload whose platform/arch differs from the running process is rejected at the first tool call.

recovery.scenario: Download the matching target explicitly, verify hashes, and re-run the installed smoke.

limitations: Hash verification does not make writable deployment files safe to execute.
Unused cached versions require manual removal.
A provider added by a newer consumer installation can lack generated metadata until regeneration.
